prime.problem: A paper whose code and data can't be checked is hard to trust, but a release that pushes everything can redistribute other people's data without permission. Without sorting files by who made them and under what terms, you either hide your evidence or ship something you had no right to ship.
prime.fits: The last step of the capstone. It takes the licensing caveat first met in Lab: audit 21,000 public runs and the figures from Write it against the evidence, and turns them into a release list and a pitch.
expect: labels keyed by ids instead of quoted text
a release tarball sized before it's built
a pitch with one sentence waiting on the sweep
prime.goal: Put every file in the repo into one of three piles with a reason, show the released labels can't reconstruct the trajectories, and write a pitch paragraph whose every number is sourced.

attend: Why can the paper publish per-submission rates about SWE-bench runs but not the runs themselves?
What property of handlabels.json makes it safe to release, and which of its blocks still need reading by hand?
Why are the Codex and OpenCode prompts publishable while Claude Code's is not even in the repo?
Which sentence of the pitch can't be written yet, and what must not be put in its place?
Why exclude the work/ folders from the run tarball, and what does that do to its size?

must: SWE-bench/experiments has no LICENSE and the redistribution issue is unanswered → you can't safely re-share its trajectories → publish aggregates and id-keyed labels, and let readers re-download through fetch.py

Labels keyed by (submission, instance_id) hold booleans and short verdicts, not agent text → they can't reconstruct the source runs → they join your claims to the public data without redistributing it

The transplanted prompts are Apache-2.0 (Codex) and MIT (OpenCode) → they can ship with attribution, and PROVENANCE.md pins repo, commit and hash → a reader can confirm the arms used the real prompts; Claude Code's is proprietary, so no Claude arm and no copy

Readers judge a result by one paragraph and its figures → the pitch must lead with what's measured now (the 21,438-run decomposition) and take its causal sentence only from the registered analysis → quoting the exploratory tampering lead as the result would undo the pre-registration
elevated: Each run folder keeps a workspace copy that is regenerable from the task and the diff → excluding work/ and prefix_work/ shrinks the baseline pilot from 52 MB on disk to 1.4 MB compressed → the sweep's runs fit a release asset
reference: 115 tracked files at e787d63; .gitignore ignores runs/, tasks/generated/, .venv/
pilot/data is 7.1 GB and ignored by pilot/.gitignore; runs/ is 164 MB
handlabels.json: ack_labels 148 booleans, relevant_robust_audit 52 verdicts, other_sc_audit 55 entries
nebius/SWE-agent-trajectories is CC-BY-4.0; GitHub issue #462 on SWE-bench/experiments
analysis/run_main.py writes results/main.md and the figures (addendum 3, ce5bd74)

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the three piles and put at least two concrete files or folders in each, with the reason they're there. Then write the pitch's first two sentences from memory.
checklist: publish: your code, the transplanted Codex/OpenCode prompts with attribution, results.md and fig1, aggregates, handlabels.json
point to: the SWE-bench trajectories and logs in pilot/data, via fetch.py
author decides or keep: your own runs/ tarball; Claude Code's prompt is not in the repo at all
pitch: honest misses 15.6% vs genuine self-contradiction 0.17% (about 90 to 1), 36.7% untested; then the branching, pre-registered causal test

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between 'publish' and 'point to' using one file from each pile in this repo.
answer: publish: something you made and may license, e.g. handlabels.json or the checker
point to: something others made without terms that allow redistribution, e.g. the SWE-bench trajectories
pointing to means a script (fetch.py) that re-downloads it from the original location

retrieve.q: Walk through how a reader would reproduce the pilot's 14 hand-verified cases from what you release.
answer: run fetch.py to download the trajectories from the public S3 bucket and GitHub
run parse.py, detect.py and analyze.py from the released code
join the released handlabels.json by (submission, instance_id) to see each verdict

retrieve.q: You could release your sweep's full run folders or only the compressed trajectories without workspaces. What does each cost?
answer: full folders: larger, and the workspaces are regenerable anyway
without workspaces: 52 MB becomes 1.4 MB for the baseline pilot, still enough to re-score every run
either way it's the author's call, after checking the model provider's terms on sharing outputs

compare.q: That lab warned you not to redistribute raw trajectories even in your own copy of the lab. How does this card turn the same warning into a release plan?
answer: the lab stated the rule; this card sorts every file against it
it adds a check that the released labels hold ids and short verdicts only
it adds the prompt licences and the author's decision on posting

compare.q: Pre-registration fixed the analysis before the data. What does it fix about the pitch, and what would break it?
answer: the pitch's causal sentence must come from the registered confirmatory analysis
quoting the baseline's exploratory +20 point tampering lead as the finding would break it
a null is reported with its interval, and the decomposition carries the pitch

predict.q: Suppose GitHub issue #462 gets a maintainer reply saying the logs may be redistributed under CC-BY. Predict which of this card's decisions change and which stay.
predict.answer: The 'point to' pile could become 'publish with attribution', so a cleaned subset of trajectories (for example the 105 task-relevant cases) could ship for reviewers. The id-keyed labels, the fetch script and the decision about your own runs stay as they are, and the author still decides whether and when to post. You'd still check that the hand-check dumps contain nothing beyond the newly licensed data.

apply.task: In a scratch clone, list every tracked file under pilot/ with git ls-files pilot and assign each to a pile with a one-line reason. Then run the step 2 script and read the two blocks that are not id-keyed.
apply.done: You have a pile for each of the 12 tracked files under pilot/ (at e787d63: .gitignore, five .py pipeline scripts plus handcheck.py, fig1.pdf, fig1.png, handlabels.json, results.md, sample150.txt), and a note saying whether detector_round3 and detector_round2_dev contain any quoted agent text.
apply.hint: sample150.txt lists task ids for the 150-task sample; ids are the same kind of thing the labels are keyed by.
